To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the composition of bird assembles in the Swiss Alps is determined by environmental filtering, (ii) the phylogenetic structure of these communities decreases with elevation, and (iii) species traits are not phylogenetically structured and do not mediate the environmental filtering of the bird assemblages.

(1) phylogenetic diversity is reduced in high elevation communities, but phylogenetic clustering is weak; (2) the distribution of species across plots is related to elevation and habitat type, but this relationship is not mediated by the evolutionary relatedness among species; (3) high elevation communities have lower fecundity and reduced lifespan; and (4) the phylogenetic signal in the traits was weak and only lifespan showed significant phylogenetic signal.
the phylogenetic composition of bird communities in the Alps does not change with elevation, but species assemblages at high elevations are composed of taxa with lower reproductive rates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how phylogenetic and environmental filters affect the assembly of bird communities along an elevational transect.
the role of environmental gradients as filters in community assembly, and how the phylogenetically structured variation in traits is associated with the distribution of species in these gradients.
the role of evolutionary history and the environment in shaping community structure, and how these factors influence the response of species to environmental changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

evolutionary constraints are not a significant driver of bird community assembly in the Swiss Alps, and that phylogeny does not provide a good proxy for trait-based responses to environmental filtering.
phylogenetic relationships and trait-based community structure are not strongly linked, but that environmental factors may still have an effect on trait distribution.
, while phylogenetic relationships do not play a major role in structuring Alpine bird communities, they may be important for the persistence of the species within the community.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
phylogeny is not a good proxy for life-history traits in this system, but the traits themselves are related to environmental filtering, which is a key driver of community assembly.
the community structure of bird species in the Swiss Alps is not phylogenetically constrained, but rather determined by environmental factors.
the Alpine bird community is composed of species that are less resilient to environmental changes, and that this is not due to their phylogenetic relatedness.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, although the phylogeny of a community may provide a useful framework to understand the evolutionary history of a group, it is not necessarily the best predictor of the community response to environmental change.
the phylogenetic signal of traits is not necessarily a good proxy for the phylogenetic structure of assemblages.
the response of communities to environmental changes may be driven by traits, which are not constrained by the phylogenies of the species involved.
